screens.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) for Developers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build a developer’s working understanding of AWS Identity and Access Management. IAM is how you control authentication — who signs in — and authorization — what that identity can do. For a developer, the most important parts are users, groups, roles and policies, and how they work together to give applications secure, short-lived access to resources. You will see how roles replace long-lived secrets, why policies are written as explicit allow and deny statements, and how the Principle of Least Privilege reduces blast radius. We’ll ground the ideas with concrete examples, including a read-only S3 policy you can use in a lab, and practical checks like enabling MFA and avoiding root account usage. By the end you should be able to choose the right IAM entity for a Lambda or EC2 workload, write a narrowly scoped policy, and spot common mistakes. Think of IAM as the guardrail system for your cloud infrastructure — it keeps your code and data safe while letting applications do their jobs.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › IAM Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Identity and Access Management for Developers

Learn the identities you create, the policies that grant permissions, and safe patterns for applications to access AWS services without long-lived credentials.

In this lesson
Users, Groups & Roles

Who represents people and services, and how to group them for easier access control.

Coming up
Policies & Least Privilege

How to write policies that allow only needed actions on specific resources.

Practice
MFA, rotation, audit

Concrete steps to secure root and user accounts, rotate keys and monitor activity.

Explore Key Topics
Users & Groups
Manage people and assign permissions at scale using groups.
Roles & Temporary Creds
Let services assume roles to avoid long-lived keys on instances or functions.
Policies & Best Practices
Write narrow policies, enable MFA, and audit activity with CloudTrail.
Concept Map
Users, groups, roles, policies — how they connect
User
Person or app with long-lived credentials
Role
Assumed identity that issues temporary credentials
Group
Collection of users sharing permissions
Policy
JSON rules that allow or deny actions

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice and assessments. First, you will explain the core IAM components: what an IAM user, group, role, and policy represent and when to use each. That helps you choose the correct identity for a human, a service, or an application. Second, you will differentiate identity-based policies versus resource-based policies. Knowing the difference prevents misapplied permissions and clarifies who owns the policy decision. Third, you will apply the Principle of Least Privilege: write and test policies that grant only the actions and resources required. This reduces risk and is a tangible discipline you’ll practice in the lab. Finally, you will understand operational best practices such as enabling multi-factor authentication, using roles and temporary credentials for compute workloads, rotating keys, and monitoring IAM activity. These objectives prepare you to secure accounts and design app permissions that are maintainable, auditable, and safe.

screens.title: What is IAM and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Identity and Access Management is the control plane that decides who can perform which actions on your AWS resources. Define an IAM identity as a subject that can be authenticated — a person, a machine, or a service — and a policy as the set of rules that determine what that identity is allowed to do. For developers, IAM is not an optional admin concern: it determines whether your app can read from a database, write to a storage bucket, or call other services. A concrete example: a web service that needs to read images from S3 should obtain permissions via a role assumed by the compute environment, rather than embedding access keys in configuration files. A common misconception is treating IAM as only user management; instead, it is a runtime authorization system that also controls service-to-service access. Remember that explicit Deny wins over Allow in policy evaluation, so restrictive denies can be a safety net when needed. The core takeaway is to design identities and permissions so that code can do its job with the smallest necessary permission set, minimizing risk and simplifying audits. What small permission could you remove from your next deployment to reduce exposure?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IAM controls authentication and authorization; treat it as a runtime permission layer for both humans and services.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is IAM
Core Concept

IAM in one definition

IAM is the AWS service that authenticates identities and evaluates policies to authorize actions on resources.

Who are identities?
Users, groups, roles — any subject that can be authenticated.
What are policies?
JSON documents that Allow or Deny specific actions on named resources under optional conditions.
Why this matters for developers
Permissions determine whether your code can succeed in production; misuse leads to breached data or outages.
Concrete example

An EC2 instance that needs to read from an S3 bucket should assume a role with s3:GetObject permission for that bucket. This avoids embedding access keys on the instance and enables automatic temporary credentials rotation.

Common misconception
IAM is only for people. In reality it also governs how services interact and how applications obtain credentials.
Key takeaway
Model identities and policies early; roles and temporary credentials reduce credential risk.

screens.title: IAM Users and Groups
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM user represents a person or an application that needs long-lived credentials, such as a password for the console or access keys for the A P I. A group is a collection of users. Attach policies to the group, not each user, and you simplify permission management as team membership changes. For example, a development team can have a 'Developers' group with permissions to deploy to non-production stacks, while a separate 'SRE' group has additional operational privileges. A common developer mistake is creating per-user policies with duplicated permissions — this increases administration and makes audits harder. Another misconception is relying on access keys for services; use roles instead whenever possible. Practical steps: prefer console or CLI authentication for humans, enable MFA, and avoid embedding access keys in source control. When automating, assign the automation account to a tightly scoped group or use a role for the service. Consider periodic reviews: list group memberships, check attached policies, and remove permissions that are no longer needed. Which group would you create for your current team to minimize per-user policy clutter? IAM Users and Groups means use users for individual identities, groups to manage permissions at scale and reduce duplication.. In practical terms, how to represent people and manage permissions at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Users vs Groups
keyIdea.text: Use users for individual identities, groups to manage permissions at scale and reduce duplication.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Users & Groups
Definition

IAM User and Group

Users identify individuals or service accounts. Groups let you attach a single permission set to many users for easier management.

  • Users: have credentials and can be assigned to groups.
  • Groups: simplify permissions, reduce duplication, and support team changes.
  • Enable MFA for users with sensitive privileges and avoid embedding credentials in code.
Scenario

Your frontend team needs deploy rights to a staging bucket and read-only access to logs. Create a 'frontend-developers' group with a narrowly scoped policy, then add or remove team members without changing policies per user.

Common mistake
Assigning policies individually to users rather than grouping them. This makes audits and updates error-prone.
Key Takeaway

Group users by role or team and attach policies to the group to keep permissions consistent and maintainable.

screens.title: IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM role is an identity that can be assumed by a trusted principal: a human, an AWS service, or an identity from another account. Unlike users, roles do not have long-lived credentials. When an entity assumes a role it receives temporary security credentials that expire automatically. This is crucial for services: for example, an EC2 instance or a Lambda function can assume a role to access S3, and the platform automatically rotates the credentials. A concrete example: instead of storing access keys in configuration, attach an instance profile to an EC2 instance that gives it s3:GetObject on a specific bucket. A typical misconception is that roles are only for cross-account access; in fact roles are the recommended credential model for any AWS service needing permissions. When designing roles, scope the permissions narrowly and use condition keys when possible. A quick audit step is to list roles with attached policies and check which services are allowed to assume them. Think about your last deployment: could a role have replaced a hard-coded key to improve safety? IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials means roles provide temporary credentials for services and remove the need for hard-coded long-lived keys.. In practical terms, how roles are assumed and why they reduce credential risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Roles & Temporary Credentials
Process Flow

How a role is assumed

  1. Attach a role to a service (for EC2, via an instance profile; for Lambda, via the function role).
  2. Service requests temporary credentials from the AWS STS service to act as that role.
  3. AWS provides time-limited credentials which the service uses until they expire, then refreshes automatically.
Example

An EC2 instance that reads S3 objects should use an instance role with s3:GetObject for the specific bucket instead of embedded keys. This prevents credential leakage from the instance.

Misconception
Temporary credentials are optional. They are best practice for all services to avoid long-lived secrets.
Pro tip
Use conditions in the trust policy to limit which principals can assume the role and from where.
Quick audit

List roles, check their trust relationships, and review attached policies for least privilege. Remove unused roles to reduce risk.

Key Takeaway

Prefer roles for services; they give temporary rotated credentials and reduce credential exposure.

screens.title: IAM Policies: Effect, Action, Resource
screens.narratorSegment: An IAM policy is a JSON document made up of statements that declare permissions. Each statement contains an Effect, which is either Allow or Deny; an Action or list of Actions that name the A P I operations; and a Resource or list of resource ARNs the statement applies to. Conditions can further constrain when the statement is evaluated, for example by source IP or MFA presence. For example, to allow listing and reading objects from a specific S3 bucket, a statement would set Effect to Allow, Action to s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject, and Resource to the bucket ARN and its objects. A frequent developer error is to use Action: "*" and Resource: "*" which grants excessive privileges and violates least privilege. Another subtle point: explicit Deny always takes precedence over Allow, so you can use Deny to ensure certain actions remain forbidden. Practically, author policies by starting with the smallest action set and expanding only as necessary, and test with a staging user or role to confirm behavior before deploying it to production. IAM Policies: Effect, Action, Resource means policies use effect, action, resource and optional conditions. start narrow and test before widening permissions.. In practical terms, understand the json elements that grant or deny permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Policies use Effect, Action, Resource and optional Conditions. Start narrow and test before widening permissions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Policy Structure
Definition

Key fields in a policy

Effect: Allow or Deny. Deny overrides Allows.
Action: Named API operations like s3:GetObject.
Resource: ARN(s) the action applies to, such as a bucket or object path.
Condition: Optional constraints such as source IP or MFA requirement.
Practical rule

Always replace wildcards with the minimal actions and explicit ARNs required by the application.

Concrete example

Allow listing and getting objects for a single bucket by listing both the bucket ARN and the bucket's object ARNs. This ensures listing is allowed on the bucket while object retrieval is allowed only for objects in that bucket.

Common mistake
Using Action: '*' and Resource: '*' grants far more than needed and creates a serious security risk.
Key Takeaway

Compose policies with explicit Effect, Action and Resource entries and validate them with a test principal.

screens.title: Identity-based vs Resource-based Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Identity-based policies and resource-based policies are complementary ways to express permissions. Identity-based policies are attached to users, groups, or roles and define what that identity may do across resources. Resource-based policies are attached directly to resources, such as an S3 bucket, and define which principals can access that resource and what actions they can perform. A clear example: an identity-based policy attached to a role might allow s3:GetObject on a specific bucket; a bucket policy (resource-based) might allow a cross-account IAM user to put objects into the bucket. Use resource-based policies when you want the resource owner to control access decisions, or to allow cross-account access without changing the caller's identity policies. Beware of confusion: granting permission on the identity without the resource allowing access may still fail if the resource blocks the principal. To test behavior, try a scenario where a user has an Allow in their identity policy but the resource policy includes an explicit Deny — the Deny wins. Which model fits your integration: does the resource owner need to enable access, or should the caller be granted permission centrally?

keyIdea.text: Identity-based policies follow the principal; resource-based policies let the resource owner decide who can access it, useful for cross-account access.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Identity vs Resource Policies
Identity-based

Attached to user, group, or role

Defines what the identity is allowed to do across resources in the account or other accounts.

Use when you manage who can perform actions centrally, such as granting EC2 launch permissions.
Resource-based

Attached to the resource itself

The resource owner decides which principals may access the resource, commonly used by S3 bucket policies and SQS queue policies.

Ideal for cross-account access where the resource owner needs explicit control.
Scenario

If you need a user from another account to upload objects to your bucket without changing their identity policies, add a bucket policy that grants the other account's principal PutObject on your bucket. This keeps control with the resource owner.

Key Takeaway

Choose identity-based policy when you control the principal; choose resource-based when the resource owner must authorize access or enable cross-account principals.

screens.title: Applying the Principle of Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: The Principle of Least Privilege means granting the minimum permissions required for a task. Follow a simple process to apply it: first inventory the actions your application performs; second, map those actions to specific A P I operations and resources; third, author a policy that lists only those actions and resource ARNs; fourth, test the policy with a staging principal; finally, monitor and iterate. For example, if a function only needs to write logs and upload files to a single S3 bucket, grant logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents plus s3:PutObject on that bucket only. Avoid using wildcards on Action or Resource. A misconception is that least privilege will break development velocity; instead, it prevents escalations and forces explicit design thinking. Testing should include negative tests: attempt an action outside the allowed set and confirm it fails. Periodic reviews are essential because application behavior changes over time and permissions may need adjustment. The practical question to ask is: what is the single additional permission you would remove right now to reduce your blast radius? Applying the Principle of Least Privilege means design policies from observed needs, test with staging principals, then monitor and refine regularly.. In practical terms, steps to design, implement, and validate minimal permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least Privilege
keyIdea.text: Design policies from observed needs, test with staging principals, then monitor and refine regularly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Least Privilege
Process

5-step workflow

  1. List exact operations your app calls in production.
  2. Map operations to IAM Actions and Resource ARNs.
  3. Author a policy with only those Actions and Resources.
  4. Test with a staging user or role and run negative tests.
  5. Audit and reduce permissions over time.
Concrete example

A function that only uploads images needs s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::my-app-images/* and no other S3 permissions. Start there, then add only what testing requires.

Negative test
Attempt an action outside the policy and confirm you get AccessDenied — this validates the scope.
Key Takeaway

Be conservative: grant only what is needed, test that denied actions truly fail, and schedule regular reviews.

screens.title: S3 Read-Only Policy Example
screens.narratorSegment: Now we’ll walk through a concrete identity-based policy that grants read-only access to one S3 bucket. The policy illustrates the key fields: Version, Statement, Effect set to Allow, Action listing the permitted A P I calls, and Resource listing the bucket and its objects. Use this pattern to scope permissions precisely. After applying the policy to a user or role, verify that listing and get-object calls succeed while delete or put operations fail. A common error when copying examples is forgetting the bucket object ARN ending in /* — without it, get object calls may be denied. Another point: test the policy with the AWS CLI in a sandbox profile to confirm behavior before deploying to production. The example shown in the code block is ready to be copied into the console's policy editor; replace the bucket name with your own. Finally, ask yourself: does this policy expose any more than read-only operations for that bucket? If yes, tighten it. S3 Read-Only Policy Example means a minimal s3 read-only policy lists only s3:listbucket and s3:getobject and specifies the bucket arn and its object arns.. In practical terms, walk through a minimal identity-based policy for a specific bucket. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Policy JSON
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [

        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": [

      ]
    }
  ]
}

screens.title: Account Security: MFA, Root Account, and Key Rotation
screens.narratorSegment: Security hygiene matters as much as correct policies. First, enable Multi-Factor Authentication for the root account and all privileged IAM users — MFA adds a second factor that drastically reduces the risk of credential-based compromise. Second, never use the root account for daily tasks. Create an administrative IAM user for routine administration and reserve the root account for account-level operations only. Third, rotate access keys periodically when they exist; for programmatic access prefer temporary credentials via roles whenever possible. A practical sequence: enable MFA on the root, create an admin user with MFA enabled, avoid storing credentials in code or repositories, and build automation that uses roles to assume permissions. A common false comfort is thinking passwords alone suffice; modern attackers can obtain passwords, so MFA is essential. Monitoring workflow

screens.title: Common IAM Mistakes Developers Make
screens.narratorSegment: Developers frequently make a set of predictable mistakes when using IAM, and recognizing them will keep your environment safer. First, granting overly permissive policies with Action: '*' and Resource: '*' is the most common and severe error; it violates least privilege and can allow lateral movement. Second, hardcoding access keys in source code or configuration exposes credentials to version control and leaks. Third, sharing root account credentials or using the root account for routine tasks increases exposure since the root account has full control. Fourth, failing to enable MFA leaves accounts susceptible to password-only attacks. Fifth, misunderstanding policy evaluation — not realizing that an explicit Deny overrides Allow — can create both security gaps and debugging confusion. For each mistake, apply a mitigation: replace wildcards with explicit actions, switch to roles for services, enable MFA and administrative IAM users, rotate credentials and audit policies regularly. Try a quick checklist: do you have any policies with '*' actions, any undiscovered keys in repos, or root usage logs? Fix those items first to reduce risk. Developer pitfalls
  • Overly permissive policies: Wildcards grant excessive access and should be replaced with explicit actions.
  • Hardcoded credentials: Keys in code are easy to leak; use roles instead.

  • No MFA: Accounts without MFA are more vulnerable to compromise.

  • Audit policies and remove wildcards.

When you review an account, start by finding policies with '*' actions and any access keys older than your rotation policy.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build a developer’s working understanding of AWS Identity and Access Management. IAM is how you control authentication — who signs in — and authorization — what that identity can do. For a developer, the most important parts are users, groups, roles and policies, and how they work together to give applications secure, short-lived access to resources. You will see how roles replace long-lived secrets, why policies are written as explicit allow and deny statements, and how the Principle of Least Privilege reduces blast radius. We’ll ground the ideas with concrete examples, including a read-only S3 policy you can use in a lab, and practical checks like enabling MFA and avoiding root account usage. By the end you should be able to choose the right IAM entity for a Lambda or EC2 workload, write a narrowly scoped policy, and spot common mistakes. Think of IAM as the guardrail system for your cloud infrastructure — it keeps your code and data safe while letting applications do their jobs.

These objectives focus your practice and assessments. First, you will explain the core IAM components: what an IAM user, group, role, and policy represent and when to use each. That helps you choose the correct identity for a human, a service, or an application. Second, you will differentiate identity-based policies versus resource-based policies. Knowing the difference prevents misapplied permissions and clarifies who owns the policy decision. Third, you will apply the Principle of Least Privilege: write and test policies that grant only the actions and resources required. This reduces risk and is a tangible discipline you’ll practice in the lab. Finally, you will understand operational best practices such as enabling multi-factor authentication, using roles and temporary credentials for compute workloads, rotating keys, and monitoring IAM activity. These objectives prepare you to secure accounts and design app permissions that are maintainable, auditable, and safe.

This second objectives slide maps the chapter to the lab steps and assessment ideas. You will create an IAM user with a custom read-only S3 policy, test the user with the AWS CLI, and verify that permissions are limited as expected. In assessment scenarios you should be able to pick the correct IAM entity — for example, choosing a role for a Lambda function — and explain why that choice removes the need for long-lived credentials. You will also practice spotting overly permissive policies and explaining why they violate least privilege. Finally, you will learn to use CloudTrail and periodic audits to detect and remove stale permissions. These tasks give you both conceptual and procedural competence: know the components, choose the right entity, and apply secure operations in a real account.

Identity and Access Management is the control plane that decides who can perform which actions on your AWS resources. Define an IAM identity as a subject that can be authenticated — a person, a machine, or a service — and a policy as the set of rules that determine what that identity is allowed to do. For developers, IAM is not an optional admin concern: it determines whether your app can read from a database, write to a storage bucket, or call other services. A concrete example: a web service that needs to read images from S3 should obtain permissions via a role assumed by the compute environment, rather than embedding access keys in configuration files. A common misconception is treating IAM as only user management; instead, it is a runtime authorization system that also controls service-to-service access. Remember that explicit Deny wins over Allow in policy evaluation, so restrictive denies can be a safety net when needed. The core takeaway is to design identities and permissions so that code can do its job with the smallest necessary permission set, minimizing risk and simplifying audits. What small permission could you remove from your next deployment to reduce exposure?

An IAM user represents a person or an application that needs long-lived credentials, such as a password for the console or access keys for the A P I. A group is a collection of users. Attach policies to the group, not each user, and you simplify permission management as team membership changes. For example, a development team can have a 'Developers' group with permissions to deploy to non-production stacks, while a separate 'SRE' group has additional operational privileges. A common developer mistake is creating per-user policies with duplicated permissions — this increases administration and makes audits harder. Another misconception is relying on access keys for services; use roles instead whenever possible. Practical steps: prefer console or CLI authentication for humans, enable MFA, and avoid embedding access keys in source control. When automating, assign the automation account to a tightly scoped group or use a role for the service. Consider periodic reviews: list group memberships, check attached policies, and remove permissions that are no longer needed. Which group would you create for your current team to minimize per-user policy clutter? IAM Users and Groups means use users for individual identities, groups to manage permissions at scale and reduce duplication.. In practical terms, how to represent people and manage permissions at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An IAM role is an identity that can be assumed by a trusted principal: a human, an AWS service, or an identity from another account. Unlike users, roles do not have long-lived credentials. When an entity assumes a role it receives temporary security credentials that expire automatically. This is crucial for services: for example, an EC2 instance or a Lambda function can assume a role to access S3, and the platform automatically rotates the credentials. A concrete example: instead of storing access keys in configuration, attach an instance profile to an EC2 instance that gives it s3:GetObject on a specific bucket. A typical misconception is that roles are only for cross-account access; in fact roles are the recommended credential model for any AWS service needing permissions. When designing roles, scope the permissions narrowly and use condition keys when possible. A quick audit step is to list roles with attached policies and check which services are allowed to assume them. Think about your last deployment: could a role have replaced a hard-coded key to improve safety? IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials means roles provide temporary credentials for services and remove the need for hard-coded long-lived keys.. In practical terms, how roles are assumed and why they reduce credential risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An IAM policy is a JSON document made up of statements that declare permissions. Each statement contains an Effect, which is either Allow or Deny; an Action or list of Actions that name the A P I operations; and a Resource or list of resource ARNs the statement applies to. Conditions can further constrain when the statement is evaluated, for example by source IP or MFA presence. For example, to allow listing and reading objects from a specific S3 bucket, a statement would set Effect to Allow, Action to s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject, and Resource to the bucket ARN and its objects. A frequent developer error is to use Action: "*" and Resource: "*" which grants excessive privileges and violates least privilege. Another subtle point: explicit Deny always takes precedence over Allow, so you can use Deny to ensure certain actions remain forbidden. Practically, author policies by starting with the smallest action set and expanding only as necessary, and test with a staging user or role to confirm behavior before deploying it to production. IAM Policies: Effect, Action, Resource means policies use effect, action, resource and optional conditions. start narrow and test before widening permissions.. In practical terms, understand the json elements that grant or deny permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Identity-based policies and resource-based policies are complementary ways to express permissions. Identity-based policies are attached to users, groups, or roles and define what that identity may do across resources. Resource-based policies are attached directly to resources, such as an S3 bucket, and define which principals can access that resource and what actions they can perform. A clear example: an identity-based policy attached to a role might allow s3:GetObject on a specific bucket; a bucket policy (resource-based) might allow a cross-account IAM user to put objects into the bucket. Use resource-based policies when you want the resource owner to control access decisions, or to allow cross-account access without changing the caller's identity policies. Beware of confusion: granting permission on the identity without the resource allowing access may still fail if the resource blocks the principal. To test behavior, try a scenario where a user has an Allow in their identity policy but the resource policy includes an explicit Deny — the Deny wins. Which model fits your integration: does the resource owner need to enable access, or should the caller be granted permission centrally?

The Principle of Least Privilege means granting the minimum permissions required for a task. Follow a simple process to apply it: first inventory the actions your application performs; second, map those actions to specific A P I operations and resources; third, author a policy that lists only those actions and resource ARNs; fourth, test the policy with a staging principal; finally, monitor and iterate. For example, if a function only needs to write logs and upload files to a single S3 bucket, grant logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents plus s3:PutObject on that bucket only. Avoid using wildcards on Action or Resource. A misconception is that least privilege will break development velocity; instead, it prevents escalations and forces explicit design thinking. Testing should include negative tests: attempt an action outside the allowed set and confirm it fails. Periodic reviews are essential because application behavior changes over time and permissions may need adjustment. The practical question to ask is: what is the single additional permission you would remove right now to reduce your blast radius? Applying the Principle of Least Privilege means design policies from observed needs, test with staging principals, then monitor and refine regularly.. In practical terms, steps to design, implement, and validate minimal permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Developers frequently make a set of predictable mistakes when using IAM, and recognizing them will keep your environment safer. First, granting overly permissive policies with Action: '*' and Resource: '*' is the most common and severe error; it violates least privilege and can allow lateral movement. Second, hardcoding access keys in source code or configuration exposes credentials to version control and leaks. Third, sharing root account credentials or using the root account for routine tasks increases exposure since the root account has full control. Fourth, failing to enable MFA leaves accounts susceptible to password-only attacks. Fifth, misunderstanding policy evaluation — not realizing that an explicit Deny overrides Allow — can create both security gaps and debugging confusion. For each mistake, apply a mitigation: replace wildcards with explicit actions, switch to roles for services, enable MFA and administrative IAM users, rotate credentials and audit policies regularly.
